text: Every script so far has hardcoded its values — a fixed hostname, a fixed threshold. A real tool takes input from whoever runs it, like server-health --host nbr-db-01 --threshold 95. This lesson builds exactly that, from the ground up: a real Northbridge server-health command-line tool, using the standard library's argparse module.

argparse separates two kinds of arguments. A positional argument, like the hostname here, is required and identified purely by its position. An optional argument, like --threshold, is identified by its flag and usually carries a default — leave it off and args.threshold just falls back to 90.

Some optional arguments don't take a value at all — they're flags. Define one with action="store_true", and its presence alone is the signal: args.verbose comes back True if --verbose was passed on the command line, False if it wasn't. No extra value, no quotes, just the flag itself on or off.

Put those pieces together and you get real logic driven entirely by what the user typed: check_health looks up the host's usage, compares it to the threshold argument, and prints an alert or an OK message — no hardcoded host or number anywhere in the function itself.

That's the full shape of a CLI tool: define your arguments, call parse_args to read them off the command line, get a --help screen generated automatically from those same definitions, and finish by calling sys.exit with a code — zero for success, and a distinct nonzero number for each specific kind of failure you want the caller to be able to tell apart.
Next up, you'll make sure this same tool actually logs what it's doing — with the logging module — instead of failing silently when something goes wrong.
